margaret.title: A modern beginning in 1967
margaret.cue: Margaret River’s commercial wine story began with Vasse Felix in 1967.
margaret.detail: Dr Tom Cullity founded Vasse Felix after scientific work helped identify the area’s winegrowing promise. Moss Wood followed in 1969. That sequence gives this Cabernet a useful historical setting: a comparatively young wine region shaped by deliberate choices about where to plant. The vineyard story began with observation and experimentation before the region became a familiar name on wine lists.
margaret.question: How would you introduce a young region without making the wine sound inexperienced?

henschke.title: Seven acres, one remembered grower
henschke.cue: Henry’s Seven remembers Henry Evans, who planted seven acres at Keyneton in 1853.
henschke.detail: Henschke’s account follows Evans and his wife Sarah, who closed the winery in 1868 after his death. The modern wine is a Barossa blend of Shiraz, Grenache, Mataro and Viognier. The producer’s 2024 page supplies this historical context; its vintage-specific proportions are not transferred to an unidentified bottle. The name remembers a vineyard beginning, rather than seven grape varieties or seven years of ageing.
henschke.question: What does the seven in the wine’s name actually refer to?

burgundy.title: A landscape divided into names
burgundy.cue: Burgundy’s Côte d’Or is a patchwork of named vineyard parcels called Climats.
burgundy.detail: These parcels combine particular growing conditions with generations of human decisions. Walls, paths and settlements are part of that cultural landscape. UNESCO’s inscription concerns the Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune, where Pinot Noir and Chardonnay connect individual plots to a long history of comparison. A small place name can therefore carry more meaning than a broad grape name: it locates the wine within an inherited map.
burgundy.question: Which words on this label name the village, parcel and producer?

chablis.title: A sea beneath the vineyard
chablis.cue: Chablis rests on limestone and marl formed in an ancient marine environment.
chablis.detail: The regional body distinguishes Kimmeridgian and younger Portlandian formations. Chablis, Premier Cru and Grand Cru vineyards are mainly on Kimmeridgian hillsides; Petit Chablis is mainly associated with Portlandian ground. Tiny oyster fossils make the geological story tangible. The comparison is about the vineyard’s physical setting. A tasting word such as mineral is an impression to describe, rather than evidence that dissolved rock tastes directly of the bedrock.
chablis.question: Can you explain the landscape without claiming that a fossil becomes a flavour?

bordeaux.title: One region, several grape voices
bordeaux.cue: Bordeaux builds identity from grape varieties adapted to different growing conditions.
bordeaux.detail: A regional blend is a set of choices, not one universal recipe. The Bordeaux Wine Council connects its varieties with differences in terroir and microclimate. Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc belong to the region’s red vocabulary; Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon help explain its whites. The château name identifies the producer while the appellation narrows the place. Read both before applying a general Bordeaux description to a particular cuvée.
bordeaux.question: What can the regional name tell you, and what requires this bottle’s technical sheet?

rhone.title: Follow the river north and south
rhone.cue: The Rhône changes its grape vocabulary as you travel along the valley.
rhone.detail: Syrah anchors the northern red appellations; white varieties include Viognier and Marsanne. In the south, Grenache commonly joins Syrah, Mourvèdre and other partners. The distinction helps explain why Hermitage, Côte-Rôtie and Châteauneuf-du-Pape should not be introduced as interchangeable Rhône reds. Begin with the appellation and its part of the valley, then ask what this producer selected and how the named cuvée differs from its neighbours.
rhone.question: Locate this wine in the northern or southern Rhône before discussing its blend.

chianti.title: The black rooster marks a place
chianti.cue: Chianti Classico’s black rooster connects the wine to a defined Tuscan territory.
chianti.detail: The emblem draws on a regional historical symbol and has appeared across Chianti Classico bottles since 2005. Sangiovese leads the wines’ identity. Read the words Classico carefully: they are part of the place name, not merely a compliment. Producer, cuvée and any category such as Riserva or Gran Selezione add information after origin; they do not replace the experience of tasting the particular release.
chianti.question: Introduce the place before using a category as a shorthand for quality.

langhe.title: Several wines share these hills
langhe.cue: The Langhe’s appellations describe a family of wines, not a single Piedmont style.
langhe.detail: Barolo and Barbaresco sit alongside other protected names, including wines named for Barbera and Dolcetto, as well as broader Langhe bottlings. This diversity makes the denomination on the label essential. Nebbiolo, Barbera, Arneis and Moscato entries in this collection are useful comparisons because sharing a regional address does not mean sharing a grape, a texture or a winemaking aim. Start by reading the full name before reaching for a familiar regional stereotype.
langhe.question: Compare two Piedmont labels: which part describes the grape and which the origin?

montalcino.title: Two expressions of Montalcino
montalcino.cue: Brunello and Rosso di Montalcino both centre on Sangiovese, locally called Brunello.
montalcino.detail: The consortium presents Rosso as a younger expression alongside the longer maturation of Brunello. Growers can make different selections from the same vineyard landscape. This is a useful story about decisions and time: one town and one grape can give a producer more than one voice. A Riserva or named cuvée adds another layer to investigate, while the harvest year remains separate from years spent maturing before sale.
montalcino.question: Describe Rosso and Brunello without calling one merely a cheaper version of the other.

tuscany.title: Tradition makes room for experiment
tuscany.cue: Tuscany’s modern wine story includes experiments with international grapes alongside Sangiovese.
tuscany.detail: Visit Tuscany traces a wave of experimentation in the 1970s, including Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, and follows the coastal wine routes through Bolgheri and Maremma. That history helps explain the diversity of the Tuscan entries here. It does not place every Tuscan vineyard on the coast or give every wine the same blend. Use the exact label to move from the broad regional story to this producer’s particular choice of grapes.
tuscany.question: What distinguishes this Tuscan wine from a Sangiovese-only introduction?

lebanon.title: A country with several vineyard settings
lebanon.cue: Lebanon’s wine landscape includes the Beqaa Valley and the mountains beyond it.
lebanon.detail: Massaya’s own account places most of its red and rosé vineyards in the Beqaa and its white vineyards on Mount Lebanon. This is a concrete example of how one country can hold several vineyard settings, not a sourcing claim for every Lebanese producer. With Ixsir, Mersel or another estate, the next useful question is where the grapes were grown, rather than assuming that the winery’s address identifies every vineyard in its blend.
lebanon.question: Separate the country, the winery address and the vineyard source in your explanation.

guadalupe.title: A place built around a personal memory
guadalupe.cue: Adobe Guadalupe was founded in 1997 by Tru and Don Miller in memory of their son Arlo.
guadalupe.detail: The estate brings wine, hospitality and horses together in Valle de Guadalupe. That personal beginning offers a more specific introduction to Gabriel than a generic comparison with Bordeaux. Begin with the people and the valley, then let the exact bottle establish its grape composition. The estate’s wider portfolio includes several blends, so a list of varieties grown on the property is not automatically the recipe for Gabriel.
guadalupe.question: Tell the human beginning in two sentences, then return to the wine in the glass.

dao.title: Vineyards sheltered by mountains
dao.cue: The Dão lies among mountains, with many vineyards on granite ground.
dao.detail: Wines of Portugal describes a landscape of scattered plots among pine forests, at elevations ranging from roughly 200 to 1,000 metres. That range is regional context, not the altitude of every bottle. The collection’s Alfrocheiro and Encruzado offer two different grape routes into the same place. Their names matter: learning Portugal through its own varieties is more revealing than translating every wine into an international-grape equivalent.
dao.question: How would you introduce Alfrocheiro or Encruzado without calling it a substitute for another grape?

douro.title: A river, steep slopes and terraces
douro.cue: The Douro’s vineyards follow a rugged river landscape of schist and terraces.
douro.detail: The Serra do Marão helps shelter the region from Atlantic influence. Conditions become especially dry and hot inland in summer, with cold winters. This setting supports both still wines and Port, two different paths from a shared wine landscape. A Douro red blend and a Tawny Port should therefore be connected through place while keeping their production and style distinct. The region alone cannot tell you a bottle’s sweetness or maturation.
douro.question: Explain what the still red and the Tawny share, then identify the choice that separates their styles.

cape.title: Read the Cape one district at a time
cape.cue: Hemel-en-Aarde and Swartland tell different stories within South Africa’s Cape winelands.
cape.detail: The industry’s regional guide separates the Hemel-en-Aarde wards near Hermanus from Swartland’s winegrowing landscape. The point is scale: South Africa is the country, while the district and ward help locate the conditions behind a wine. In this collection, Storm’s Pinot Noir and Badenhorst’s white blend make a useful contrast. Their differences cannot be reduced to a single national style or explained by grape colour alone.
cape.question: Name the specific area before describing the wine as South African.

rioja.title: Origin and ageing are different clues
rioja.cue: Rioja describes wines through both place and maturation categories.
rioja.detail: Rioja Alta, Rioja Alavesa and Rioja Oriental identify three regional zones. Ageing words such as Reserva and Gran Reserva give another kind of information. Reading the two together is more useful than treating an ageing category as a universal flavour or score. A cuvée may also draw attention to a more specific origin. Keep the producer and harvest year in the introduction so the classification does not eclipse the individual wine.
rioja.question: Which part of this label tells you where, and which part tells you about time?

ribera.title: A season of temperature contrasts
ribera.cue: Ribera del Duero’s growing season unfolds between cold winters and dry summers.
ribera.detail: The regional council describes a continental influence within a Mediterranean climate, limited rainfall and pronounced temperature contrasts. That is the environmental frame for its wines, not a fixed prediction of how one vintage tastes. Use it to explain why the harvest year matters. Then distinguish the named cuvée, estate and grape description before comparing it with another Spanish red made from Tempranillo.
ribera.question: How might a particular season complicate a simple warm-region description?

borja.title: Garnacha across different heights
borja.cue: Campo de Borja presents Garnacha through three broad altitude zones.
borja.detail: The regional council’s focus on terroir brings together land, soil, climate and vines. The zones give a useful way to imagine variation within the appellation rather than a single uniform plain. Veraton provides a named Garnacha entry into that landscape. The next step is to identify the producer’s actual vineyard selection; a regional discussion of old vines or elevation is not evidence for the age or height of every parcel used.
borja.question: What would you ask the producer to turn regional context into a precise vineyard story?

willamette.title: A region built by deliberate planting
willamette.cue: Willamette’s modern pioneers saw promise in its latitude, climate and soils.
willamette.detail: The regional association connects the valley’s Pinot Noir identity with choices made more than fifty years ago. This was a commitment to a place and a variety, followed by generations of comparison between sites. Today the valley name is only the first layer of an introduction. A vineyard or cuvée name narrows the story further; a Pinot Gris such as Daisy shows why the region should not be reduced to Pinot Noir alone.
willamette.question: Explain what the valley shares while leaving room for an individual vineyard’s differences.

sonoma.title: Coast, fog and smaller place names
sonoma.cue: Sonoma’s appellations distinguish coastal influence and different vineyard settings.
sonoma.detail: The regional guide describes Pacific fog in Russian River Valley, cool coastal conditions and the separate identity of Carneros. These are connected but not interchangeable places. Read Sonoma Valley, Sonoma Coast, Russian River or Carneros as a more useful starting point than a single California stereotype. A broad California label does not by itself establish one Sonoma appellation; confirm the exact origin before borrowing a narrower landscape story.
sonoma.question: Which place name is printed on this bottle, and how specific is it?

napa.title: A small valley with many settings
napa.cue: Napa Valley’s identity includes differences in soil, topography and local climate.
napa.detail: Its regional association treats the valley as a collection of growing environments rather than one uniform vineyard. Sub-appellation names help locate those differences. Oakville is more specific than Napa Valley, while a vineyard name can narrow the focus further. Read the label from broad origin to smaller place, then to the producer’s selection. This approach works for Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc as well as the Cabernet wines for which the valley is widely known.
napa.question: What does this label let you locate precisely, and what remains a broader regional address?

paso.title: Eleven districts within one region
paso.cue: Paso Robles contains eleven districts with different landscape and growing conditions.
paso.detail: The regional association maps hills, valleys and contrasting soils within the larger appellation. This makes Paso a useful lesson in scale: the name on a wine list can conceal considerable variation. Compare Isosceles and Booker Chardonnay as different wine decisions within the same broad region. The contrast is an invitation to ask about vineyard location and intended style, rather than assuming that every Paso wine must have the same weight or ripeness.
paso.question: Which question would help you move from the broad appellation to the actual vineyard?

seasmoke.title: A sparkling side of Sta. Rita Hills
seasmoke.cue: Sea Smoke’s Sea Spray is a Pinot Noir Blanc de Noirs sparkling wine from Sta. Rita Hills.
seasmoke.detail: The producer’s 2021 page describes estate fruit, early picking and a second fermentation in bottle. This is a documented example of one producer’s sparkling approach within the region, not the production method of every Sta. Rita Hills wine. For Donnachadh Syrah, use the shared place as a point of comparison while keeping the grape and still-wine style distinct. For Sea Spray, Pinot Noir should not lead you to expect a still red.
seasmoke.question: Explain how the same region can produce still Syrah and a pale sparkling Pinot Noir.

sancerre.title: Three useful words for the ground
sancerre.cue: Sancerre’s regional guide distinguishes terres blanches, caillottes and flint-bearing soils.
sancerre.detail: Terres blanches combine clay and limestone; caillottes describe stony limestone ground. Flint and clay appear in the eastern part of the area. These terms give the landscape a vocabulary, but the vineyard name is needed before attaching one soil description to an individual wine. Begin with the broad Sancerre identity, then investigate the site. Keep a tasting word such as flinty separate from a geological claim about what is physically present in the wine.
sancerre.question: Can you name a soil category while making clear whether this cuvée’s site has been confirmed?

pfalz.title: Vineyards beside a protective forest
pfalz.cue: The Pfalz’s vineyards benefit from the shelter of the Palatinate Forest.
pfalz.detail: The German Wine Institute places Riesling at the centre of the region’s wine identity. The landscape extends along the German Wine Route, with many individual villages and vineyard names. For this entry, Forster Kirchenstück is the specific name worth retaining in an introduction. A grape, village, site and producer each answer a different question; compressing them into German Riesling would lose the most useful distinctions.
pfalz.question: Build an introduction that preserves the site name rather than stopping at grape and country.

nahe.title: Geology changes over short distances
nahe.cue: The Nahe has an unusually varied patchwork of soils along its river and side valleys.
nahe.detail: The German Wine Institute describes slate, quartzite, volcanic formations, sandstone and loess in different parts of the region. It also distinguishes cooler upper areas from other vineyard settings. This variety explains why a generic Dönnhoff Riesling entry leaves important questions open: the exact cuvée and vineyard matter. Do not borrow the sweetness level or site history of one named release simply because the producer and grape match.
nahe.question: Which missing label detail would most improve this generic Riesling description?

santorini.title: Vines woven against the wind
santorini.cue: On Santorini, basket-shaped kouloura training helps protect grapes in a windy setting.
santorini.detail: The regional account describes volcanic ash, pumice and sand, with grapes sheltered inside the woven vine structure. That physical picture is a memorable way to introduce Assyrtiko from the island. It connects cultivation to the environment without turning a volcano into a tasting note. For Sigalas, move next to the precise cuvée and vintage; the island story provides context, while the bottle identifies the particular expression.
santorini.question: Explain the basket shape as a practical vineyard choice in one clear sentence.

gavi.title: Cortese and a route toward Genoa
gavi.cue: Gavi connects the Cortese grape with eleven municipalities in Alessandria province.
gavi.detail: The consortium’s account places the wine in a landscape with historical links toward Genoa. The full wording del Comune di Gavi narrows the origin within the broader Gavi denomination. That is the useful distinction to preserve when introducing Villa Sparina: grape, appellation, more specific place and producer belong to different layers of the name. Its memorable bottle shape is a recognition aid, while the label supplies the wine identity.
gavi.question: Explain the difference between Gavi and the additional del Comune di Gavi wording.

abruzzo.title: Between the Adriatic and the mountains
abruzzo.cue: Abruzzo’s wine landscape lies between the Adriatic Sea and major mountain ranges.
abruzzo.detail: The consortium describes the influence of Gran Sasso and Majella, ventilation and temperature differences between day and night. Inland areas have more continental conditions than the milder coastal hills. This is a setting shared by different white grapes, including the Pecorino and Trebbiano entries here. It provides a strong opening for the story while leaving the producer’s vineyard, harvest decisions and cellar practices to be established separately.
abruzzo.question: How would you describe this landscape without promising a particular aroma from the mountains or sea?

altoadige.title: Alpine shelter, southern warmth
altoadige.cue: Alto Adige combines mountain shelter with warmer air arriving from the south.
altoadige.detail: The regional body describes valleys, slopes and the contrast between day and night. This is a more useful frame for Pinot Grigio than assuming the grape always makes one simple style. With Porer and Elena Walch in the collection, compare the exact bottling and its texture, then investigate vineyard and cellar choices. Regional geography can explain the questions to ask; it cannot establish an individual wine’s skin contact, lees time or barrel treatment.
altoadige.question: Choose one difference to investigate between these two Pinot Grigio bottlings.

sicily.title: An island with its own grape vocabulary
sicily.cue: Sicily’s varieties include Grillo, a crossing of Catarratto and Zibibbo.
sicily.detail: Sicilia DOC traces Grillo’s cultivation to the end of the nineteenth century and highlights its association with the Trapani area. This is one thread in a broader island story, not the recipe for every Sicilian wine. SP68 Bianco’s Albanello and Zibibbo and the Etna sparkling entry point to other choices. Retain the actual grapes and origin on the label instead of treating Sicily as one blend or one volcanic vineyard.
sicily.question: Which grape names distinguish this bottle from the other Sicilian wines in the collection?

martinborough.title: A different New Zealand address
martinborough.cue: Martinborough belongs to Wairarapa, alongside Gladstone and Masterton.
martinborough.detail: New Zealand Winegrowers describes Martinborough as cool and dry, with free-draining soils. Pinot Noir and Sauvignon Blanc are part of the local story. Te Muna offers a useful reminder that New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc is not synonymous with Marlborough. Keep the more precise place name in the introduction, then use the wine’s aromas and texture to explain its character rather than borrowing another region’s signature description.
martinborough.question: Introduce this Sauvignon Blanc without using Marlborough as a shortcut.

rias.title: Atlantic Galicia, several subzones
rias.cue: Rías Baixas presents Albariño through five subzones in Atlantic Galicia.
rias.detail: The regional guide names Val do Salnés, O Rosal, Condado do Tea, Soutomaior and Ribeira do Ulla. The O Rosal entry in this collection also lists Loureiro and Caiño Blanco, making it a useful comparison with the Albariño-labelled wines. Shared origin does not require an identical blend. First locate the subzone if known, then distinguish varietal identity from a blend built around the same regional grape vocabulary.
rias.question: What does O Rosal add to an introduction that simply says Spanish Albariño?

rogue.title: Oregon beyond one valley
rogue.cue: Rogue Valley includes three distinct valleys with progressively warmer microclimates.
rogue.detail: The Oregon Wine Board describes a region capable of supporting both cool- and warm-climate varieties. Penner-Ash Viognier is an opportunity to widen the Oregon story beyond Willamette Pinot Noir. The state name is the broad frame; Rogue Valley is the more specific growing-region clue. Preserve that distinction before discussing the producer, and avoid treating the location of a winery as proof of where all of its grapes grew.
rogue.question: Explain why the grape origin can matter more than the producer’s postal address.

champagne.title: A wine assembled across several dimensions
champagne.cue: Champagne blending can bring together grape varieties, vineyard origins and harvest years.
champagne.detail: Reserve wines let a producer draw on earlier seasons for a non-vintage blend, while a vintage Champagne speaks through one harvest. A second fermentation in bottle creates the sparkling stage. The label’s cuvée, edition or vintage is therefore essential to the story: it identifies a particular assembly and release, not merely a famous house name. Blanc de Blancs, rosé and prestige cuvées are different directions within that shared regional framework.
champagne.question: Which words identify this release beyond the name of the Champagne house?

trento.title: A bottle-fermentation idea takes root
trento.cue: Giulio Ferrari brought a Champagne-inspired sparkling vision to Trentino in 1902.
trento.detail: Trentodoc’s account connects that beginning with the classic method, in which the sparkling fermentation happens in bottle. This gives Ferrari a story about a technique adapted to a particular place. The rosé and white entries should still be introduced separately: grape choice and cuvée identity matter within one house. The method connects them, while the individual release determines the detailed blend, maturation and tasting profile.
trento.question: Explain the shared method, then one label distinction between the white and rosé.

prosecco.title: Rustico changed its method in 1979
prosecco.cue: Nino Franco traces Rustico’s move from col fondo to the Charmat method to 1979.
prosecco.detail: The house began with Antonio Franco in 1919; later generations included Nino and Primo. Its history gives the familiar Rustico name a specific turning point rather than a timeless production story. The current wine is associated with Glera and Valdobbiadene. Keep Prosecco’s tank-based sparkling process distinct from the bottle-fermented Champagne and Trentodoc entries when explaining why the collection contains several kinds of sparkling wine.
prosecco.question: Retell Rustico’s change of method without suggesting that all sparkling wines are made the same way.

bandol.title: Mourvèdre gives Bandol a focal point
bandol.cue: Bandol’s grape vocabulary places particular importance on Mourvèdre.
bandol.detail: The regional body connects its red and rosé identity with this variety alongside other permitted grapes. Château Romassan belongs in that more specific conversation, rather than an undifferentiated account of pale southern French rosé. The name Bandol is the place to remember. Then ask how the producer builds the blend and handles the fruit for this cuvée, keeping those wine-specific choices separate from broad regional expectations.
bandol.question: What would you preserve from the Bandol story in a twenty-second rosé introduction?

chinon.title: A Loire name beside the Vienne
chinon.cue: Chinon’s vineyards follow the Vienne toward its meeting with the Loire.
chinon.detail: The regional account spans communes and different landscape positions, including gravelly and sandy terraces. Charles Joguet’s rosé offers a different route into Chinon from its better-known red-wine identity. Start with the river setting, then state the actual style in the glass. The Cabernet Franc listed here is a grape clue; it does not by itself tell you how long the skins were in contact or how the rosé was made.
chinon.question: Describe a rosé through its origin and grape before reaching for a colour comparison.

provence.title: Rosé begins as a vineyard intention
provence.cue: Provence’s regional body describes a hot, dry, windy Mediterranean growing environment.
provence.detail: The mistral helps dry the vineyard after humidity, while growers make decisions with rosé as an intended wine style. The story therefore begins before the juice reaches the cellar. Compare the collection’s named cuvées through producer, origin and texture, rather than using pale colour as a ranking system. The regional setting is shared context; it does not establish identical grapes, oak treatment or concentration for every bottle.
provence.question: How would you distinguish two of these rosés without using only colour or price?

languedoc.title: A broad southern landscape
languedoc.cue: Languedoc contains many wine identities within a broad Mediterranean setting.
languedoc.detail: The regional body presents its appellations as distinct expressions of that larger landscape. This collection places Clos du Temple rosé beside Orange Tacsum, a useful reminder that neighbouring regional labels can conceal very different winemaking aims. The broad regional discussion does not assign an AOP to either bottle. Read its actual designation and grape list before describing a more specific site, production method or classification.
languedoc.question: Separate the broad place name from the particular wine style and designation.

commandaria.title: Sun-dried Xynisteri, without fortification
commandaria.cue: Tsiakkas identifies its Commandaria as Xynisteri from Agios Mamas, made without fortification.
commandaria.detail: The producer describes a vineyard at 800 metres on limestone, grapes dried in the sun for ten days and maturation in French and American oak. These are useful, concrete details for this wine. They distinguish a documented producer method from sweeping legends about the age of Commandaria. The page lists three years of oak maturation; confirm the release before assigning a specific production duration to the bottle you are serving.
commandaria.question: Explain how drying grapes and adding spirit are different ways to approach a sweet wine.

valpo.title: Drying grapes, keeping sweetness
valpo.cue: Recioto della Valpolicella uses dried grapes and retains sweetness through its fermentation choices.
valpo.detail: The consortium describes appassimento as part of the process and a fermentation stopped while sugar remains. This offers a clear way to distinguish Recioto’s intended sweet style from a dry red made in the same broad region. For Dal Forno Romano, the producer name then narrows the enquiry to a particular selection and release. The category explains the basic method; exact drying and ageing durations still belong to the cuvée’s documentation.
valpo.question: Tell the production sequence in order: drying, fermentation, retained sweetness, maturation.

veneto.title: Read the sweet-wine label carefully
veneto.cue: The I Capitelli entry needs its exact designation checked against the producer’s label.
veneto.detail: The inherited catalogue calls it Recioto di Soave and lists Garganega. That classification has not been independently established in this review, so this chapter does not turn it into a verified appellation story. Read the bottle’s legal designation and vintage first. It is better to give a precise introduction using confirmed words than to attach another sweet wine’s production rules, drying period or origin requirements to an uncertain entry.
veneto.question: Which label words would resolve the uncertainty before serving this wine?

rieussec.title: A name remembering Carmelite monks
rieussec.cue: Carmes de Rieussec is the estate’s second Sauternes, named after the Carmes de Langon monks.
rieussec.detail: The producer links the name to the monks who owned Rieussec in the eighteenth century. Its account describes the selective harvesting of grapes affected by noble rot and distinguishes Carmes from R de Rieussec, the dry Bordeaux white. This distinction matters at the table: the similar names do not identify the same style. The producer describes Carmes with a citrus-led aromatic profile, while exact blend proportions depend on the release.
rieussec.question: Explain Carmes and R de Rieussec as two different wines, despite the shared estate name.

maconnais.title: Read past the shared Chardonnay grape
maconnais.cue: Pouilly-Fuissé and Chablis share Chardonnay, but they are different origins within Burgundy.
maconnais.detail: This catalogue entry identifies Louis Latour as the producer and Pouilly-Fuissé as the appellation. Keep those names intact when comparing it with the Côte d’Or and Chablis entries. The UNESCO Climats story shown for the Côte d’Or does not cover every Burgundy appellation. For this bottle, a vineyard, vintage and technical sheet would be needed before adding a precise soil, slope or cellar-treatment claim.
maconnais.question: Explain why sharing Chardonnay does not make two Burgundy appellations interchangeable.
